planting.note: Set divisions or nursery starts into fast-draining, rocky soil in fall rains; tolerates summer drought dormancy.

directions: A tough little clumping fern found tucked into rocky slopes and canyon walls under chaparral and oak woodland cover across much of California and into Baja California. Its leathery, blue-green to coppery fronds shrivel and appear dead through the dry season, then flush with fresh growth within days of the first autumn rains. Site it in deep to partial shade with sharp drainage, such as beneath a live oak canopy or tucked among rocks on a shaded bank, and avoid summer irrigation that can rot the rhizomes. It offers no showy bloom but provides year-round structural interest and cover for small fauna in a dry shade garden.

planting.note: Transplant in fall into the dry shade under oaks or canyon walls; established plants need little summer water.

directions: This soft-leaved, shrubby daisy relative is one of the few California natives that blooms heavily even in fairly deep shade, lighting up oak-canopied canyons and coastal sage scrub drainages with cheerful golden-yellow, two-inch flower heads nearly year-round. It occurs naturally from central to southern coastal California and into Baja California, typically along shaded stream banks, moist canyon bottoms, and beneath oaks within chaparral and coastal sage scrub mosaics. The open daisy flowers draw a range of small native bees and butterflies looking for nectar in shaded spots where little else blooms. Give it humus-rich soil and some shelter from harsh afternoon sun for the lushest growth.

planting.note: Divide and plant in fall or early spring into clay-tolerant, part-shade sites with reliable moisture.

directions: An aromatic, square-stemmed mint relative that spreads by rhizomes along shaded canyon seeps, stream margins, and damp pockets within chaparral, coastal sage scrub, and mixed-evergreen woodland from the Central Coast ranges south through the Transverse Ranges and Channel Islands. Spikes of small lavender-pink flowers appear from spring through fall and are visited by bumblebees and other native pollinators working the shaded understory. Unlike many chaparral associates it tolerates clay soil and wants more consistent moisture than the drought-adapted shrubs around it, making it useful for shaded bioswales or pond margins. Site it where runoff collects beneath oaks or bay laurel for the healthiest colonies.

planting.note: Plant divisions or starts in fall into heavier, humus-rich soil in dappled canyon shade; give occasional summer water inland.

directions: A tall, coarse-leaved perennial of shaded canyon bottoms, streamside thickets, and the moister margins of chaparral and coastal sage scrub from Southern California north into British Columbia. Narrow spires of small maroon-red, tubular flowers open from spring into summer and are a magnet for bumblebees, small wasps, and hummingbirds, while the foliage hosts Buckeye and Chalcedon Checkerspot butterfly caterpillars. It favors heavier clay soils and some shade, performing best where runoff gathers beneath oaks or bay laurel rather than on open, well-drained chaparral slopes. Cut back spent stalks after bloom to tidy the clump for next season's growth.

planting.note: Sow large seeds directly after fall rains begin, over a massive perennial tuber; vine emerges in winter and dies back by early summer.

directions: A fast-scrambling native vine that erupts from a massive underground tuber with the first winter rains, climbing over shrubs and oak litter in shaded canyon washes and the moister draws within chaparral and foothill woodland across California. Small whitish to pale-yellow flowers open in late winter and spring, feeding early native bees before the vine dies back completely by early summer to wait out the dry months. It needs no summer water once established and is best grown where its sprawling habit and spiny, grapefruit-sized fruit can be left undisturbed along a fence or fallen log. Every part of the plant, including the fruit's bitter juice, is toxic if ingested, so site it away from curious pets and children.

planting.note: Transplant in fall onto rocky, well-drained canyon slopes; let it scramble up into adjacent shrubs for support.

directions: A sprawling, half-vining shrub of brushy canyon walls and rocky chaparral slopes across cismontane Southern California and into northern Baja California, leaning on neighboring shrubs for support as it clambers upward. Tubular, pale-orange to deep-scarlet flowers cluster along the stems from late spring through summer and are a favorite of hummingbirds working shaded canyon edges. It handles considerably more shade than most chaparral shrubs, often thriving tucked beneath taller cover on the cooler, shadier side of a slope, while coastal plantings can take full sun. Give it sharp drainage and minimal summer water once roots are established.
